extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and practitioners of architecture and art criticism (travelers judging St. Mark's / Venetian architecture)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles and practical rules for designing, judging, and understanding the Venetian (Byzantine/incrusted) style of architecture, especially with respect to color, materials, ornament, and structural honesty. Focused guidance for critics, architects, and informed travelers on how to read and evaluate such buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of color as prerequisite for judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The very first requisite for true judgment of St. Mark's is the perfection of that color-faculty; one who does not perceive or delight in color cannot properly judge the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin compares a color-blind architect to a deaf man judging an orchestra. If the reader does not care for color, he should not attempt judgment of the church. This is a gatekeeping criterion: color-sense is required to appreciate incrusted architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incrusted architecture enables perfect, permanent chromatic decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The school of incrusted architecture is the only one in which perfect and permanent chromatic decoration is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the condition that the body of the edifice is brick and must be clothed with marble/stone 'armor' so that broad surfaces of durable color can be displayed; understand structure-as-body and marble-as-skin analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW I: Plinths and cornices must be light and delicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Plinths and cornices used for binding the armor are to be light and delicate; covering pieces should have certain thickness (at least two or three inches) to prevent fracture and allow for wear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These binding pieces must not be made of such proportions as to appear to take important parts of inner structure; they should be visibly incapable of severer work than assigned. Avoid designs that mistake these delicate binding members for principal structural cornices.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW I (construction detail): Armor must be tied to the mass, not merely cemented
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight of the marble 'armor' must not be trusted to cement; pieces must be connected with the mass they protect by binding cornices and string courses, and with each other, securing mutual support aided but not dependent on rivetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: merely glued/incrusted pieces that can detach. Requirement: provide mechanical binding and continuity between facing and substrate and between facing pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW II: Abandon scientific expression of inner structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Science of inner structure is to be abandoned: the body of the structure will be of inferior, incoherent materials whose mass assures sufficiency and strength; fine structural expression should be thrown into subordinate portions or directed to support the external mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt delicate internal adjustments or reduce surface to express inner construction when doing incrusted architecture; breadth of surface is needed to display color, so inner structure should be honest in mass but not refined into external expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW III: All shafts are to be solid (no incrustation or jointing)
rubrics_metrics.description: No shaft shall ever be incrusted or jointed; whatever appears probably solid must be assuredly so; shafts must be of one block and never used in jointed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the shaft's virtue depends on consolidation; cutting and adjusting incrusted coats is more labor than material saving. Practical constraint: where material is available (Venice/Egypt quarries), shafts must be flawless solid stone. Anti-pattern: using small stones or building apparent shafts of many joints as in some Northern practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shafts as expressions of wealth and honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts function as large jewels — their visible bulk and the quantity of material sacrificed to form them signify wealth and sacrifice; jointing them is a deception akin to false jewellery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spectator can measure shaft bulk by eye; inserted thin plates in walls hide thickness, but shafts reveal quantity of treasure. Anti-pattern: jointed shafts that undermine confidence in the building's ostensible richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW IV: Shafts may be independent of structural necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the shaft's importance as a jewel is the diminution of its importance as a sustaining member; shafts may be ornamental and nearly useless structurally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamental shafts should be placed to display beauty (catch sun, show veins). Symmetrical or purely scientific arrangement of pillars is often an error in this style; expect and accept pillars placed for visual effect rather than strict structural logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW V: Shafts of variable size; asymmetry acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Because value depends on bulk and blocks are limited, shafts will often be of variable size; perfect symmetry ought not to be expected and can indicate unnecessary loss by cutting down larger shafts to match smaller ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to jewellery: perfect symmetry is expensive and often impractical in architecture due to limited supply of large stones. Symmetry may be desirable in special shrines but generally accept irregular rising and falling of size as expressive and economical; anti-pattern: enforcing uniformity by cutting down prized blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply jewellery principles to exposed stonework (bookmatching veining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where veining in slabs (e.g., alabaster) is beautiful, divide the stone into thin plates and reverse one of two plates to create symmetrical figures, setting corresponding edges in contact to display veining and demonstrate they were cut from the same stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This both displays the stone's beauty and proves the honesty of the builder. Implementation: set matched veining edge-to-edge rather than dispersing matched pieces; anti-pattern: hiding matched pieces to deceive the spectator about solidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty versus deliberate deception in material display
rubrics_metrics.description: The builder should prove that thin sheeting of precious stone arises from necessity, not economy; deliberate concealment to mislead is dishonest; truth in material reveals itself under investigation while lies persistently hide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (e.g., placing matched veins edge-to-edge) should declare origin and honesty. Anti-pattern: arranging materials to mislead casual observers and conceal economy by calculated deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW VI: Decoration must be shallow in cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because covering stones are thin, carved ornament cannot be deep — at most an inch or two; ornament thus becomes more like fine drawing than sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: avoid cavernous carving and deep shadow; sculptural language must use tender pencilling and cautious restraint. Tools and temperament: chisels must not strike hard; compositions must be subdued. Expect very different character from Northern deep-carved sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer floral and lower organisms over large human forms in shallow relief
rubrics_metrics.description: In shallow bas-relief, flowers and lower animals read more intelligibly than human figures; thus ornament tends away from large human sculpture toward vegetal and small-animal motifs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because human form loses dignity when reduced to shallow outline, architects should choose ornament types that survive simplification and retain decorative clarity. Anti-pattern: forcing large human portraiture into a medium unsuited to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon naturalism; subordinate forms to architectural service and purity of line
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion as subject is reduced to abstract outline, there is a tendency to abandon naturalism and subordinate every form to its architectural function; outlines must be composed with exquisite grace, avoiding extraneous detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect restrained, carefully composed linear ornament where no line can be removed without injury; the ornamental arrangement should compensate for lack of sculptural depth. Anti-patterns: over-detailing, attempts at lifelike rendering that spoil clarity at distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of drilled hollows or black inlay for contrast and light admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, leave hollows behind covering slabs or pierce them with holes to obtain points or spaces of intense blackness which contrast with light tracery and can admit light while excluding rain and wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a safe device in incrusted buildings to introduce darkness for contrast; expect deep drill-holes or inlaid black elements used to refresh the eye amid generally light handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as primary means of architectural effect (chromatic decoration principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Color is essential in a living school of art; the Venetians' intense love of color and refined color-instinct enabled them to create abstract color harmonies and lavish decorations using mosaics, stained glass, gilding, and the tints of natural stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Southern/incrusted architecture can and should use abstract harmonies (not merely naturalistic colors tied to subject). Use permanent materials (marble, glass, gold) and exploit natural stone tints and mosaics. Example contrast: Northern practice often painted representational colors (green hawthorn etc.), whereas Southern design can ground tracery with gold or blue and use subtle mixed tones on a very small scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW VII: Impression should not depend on size; concentrate delicate work close to the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: The architecture's claims depend on delicacy of design, perfection of color, preciousness of material, and legendary interest — qualities independent of size; therefore the best work should be concentrated in comparatively small spaces visible to the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect colossal scale; delicate sculpture and subtle color harmonies require proximity. Anti-pattern: making mass large and remote, which defeats appreciation of shallow carving and subtle color.
